newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ National not discussing inflation target - Bolger.
newsitem.headline: NZ National not discussing inflation target - Bolger.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Tuesday said the government was not putting the inflation target of 0-2 percent on the table but others might.

On Monday Finance Minister Bill Birch told Reuters Television a loosening of the target band "may well be" on the agenda for coalition talks between the caretaker National Party government and nationalist New Zealand First, which holds the balance of power after the inconclusive general election.

Speaking to journalists before the first ruling National Party caucus of since the election Bolger said: "What Mr Birch said was very simple. He anticipated others would want to put that on the negotiating agenda. Why? Because they have all campaigned on different targets for inflation than the National Party. That was a perfectly rational conclusion.
"The governor of the Reserve Bank had said he could live with a slightly easier target than nought to two.

"We are actually working on a wider target range now. We are working at 0-2.5 or 0-2.6. What we want is a target range of 0-2 but accepting... that at times we might go outside that band but we aim to get back in.

"Well you could argue that was zero to three. You could go around. We are not putting that on the table. What Mr Birch said is he anticipates others would and that is perfectly rational," Bolger said.
New Zealand Finance and Expenditure committee chairman Max Bradford on Tuesday said it was unhelpful to speculate about what might be on the agenda for talks aimed at forming coalitions.

Speaking to journalists before the caucus Bradford, a strong defender of the Reserve Bank Act and the 0-2 percent inflation target, said: "I don't think at this point so early in the life of the new parliament we should be speculating on anything on what is on and what's off the table."
He said the Reserve Bank Act was bound to be one of the issues discussed at the caucus.
Speaking before the same meeting Fisheries Minister Doug Kidd said a minor adjustment to the target would not affect the general direction of economic policy.

"The general view of those who deal in those things was that a minor adjustment would not make any difference, wouldn't compromise direction. The Prime Minister's rule is that maintaining that direction is what matters. If it wouldn't have any adverse effect on direction, momentum and soundness of economic policy then it ought to be considered," Kidd said.
Labour leader Helen Clark said on Monday it was "extraordinary" for Finance Minister Bill Birch to indicate that the central bank's 0-2 percent inflation target may be negotiable in coalition talks.

"This is the man who has for six years defended that target absolutely rigidly, abused Labour when we announced a reasonable policy of broadening the range. Now he will say anything, be prepared to trade anything to get some sort of agreement to keep him in power. It really is incredible."
